aliases.name: Nurikabe
aliases.meaning: From nuru ('to plaster, paint') + kabe ('wall'); 'plastered wall'

description.summary: A Japanese yōkai of folklore from northern Kyushu that manifests as an invisible barrier blocking the path of nighttime travelers. Defeating it traditionally requires sweeping a stick along its base.
description.full: Nurikabe (塗壁, ぬりかべ, 'plastered wall') is a yōkai documented in folk traditions of northern Kyushu — particularly Onga County in former Chikuzen Province (modern Fukuoka Prefecture) and adjacent parts of Ōita Prefecture. It manifests as an invisible obstruction that suddenly bars a traveler's path on a road at night: attempts to walk around or above it fail, since the wall extends as needed. Folklorist Kunio Yanagita's 1938 collection records that 'when one is walking a path at night, suddenly the destination one is going towards turns into a wall'. The traditional remedy, recorded in the same regional sources, is to sweep a stick along the bottom of the wall — striking the top has no effect. Until 2007 the creature was thought to lack any pre-modern visual representation; that year, a c. 1660 yōkai handscroll held by Brigham Young University was identified as containing a labelled illustration of nurikabe shown as a three-eyed, dog-elephant-like beast, which is now considered the earliest extant depiction. The modern, beloved visual identity of nurikabe — a great rectangular wall with arms, legs and a face — was created by manga artist Mizuki Shigeru, who said the design grew out of a personal experience of an invisible obstruction during the Pacific War in New Guinea. Through Mizuki's GeGeGe no Kitarō series the character became a national icon. Skeptics and some cultural commentators interpret the original folk experience as a sleep-deprivation, fog or ground-hugging mist phenomenon known to nighttime travelers in the Kyushu countryside.

etymology.origin: Japanese: 塗 (nuru, 'to plaster, paint, smear') + 壁 (kabe, 'wall')
etymology.meaning: 'Plastered wall' or 'painted wall'; also rendered 塗り壁
etymology.first_use: Recorded in 20th-century Kyushu folklore collections (notably Yanagita Kunio, 1938); the BYU c. 1660 scroll labels its creature 'nurikabe', placing the term in the mid-Edo period

related_phenomena.name: Nobiagari
related_phenomena.description: Yōkai that grows taller and taller before a traveler, similarly obstructive

related_phenomena.name: Betobeto-san
related_phenomena.description: Invisible road yōkai that follows night travelers

related_phenomena.name: Tanuki
related_phenomena.description: In some regional accounts, mischievous tanuki are blamed for the same disorienting nighttime experiences

related_phenomena.name: Nurarihyon
related_phenomena.description: Similarly known mainly through Edo emaki and revived by Mizuki Shigeru

features.description: In folk accounts, the wall is unseen and felt only as resistance to forward movement
Expands in height and width to defeat attempts to climb or skirt it
Disappears or releases the traveler when its base is swept with a stick
The c. 1660 BYU scroll shows a three-eyed creature labelled nurikabe with a dog-elephant body
Modern depiction as a square wall with stubby arms, legs and a small face

physical.morphology: Traditionally non-corporeal, perceived only by touch; pre-modern art and modern manga supply the only visible morphologies.

abilities.description: Materialises as an impassable wall blocking the road ahead of a lone night traveler
Stretches taller or wider to thwart the traveler's chosen route
Causes the traveler to lose their sense of direction and walk in circles

patterns: Appears suddenly to a single traveler
Active during the late hours of the night
Departs once the lower edge is struck or swept with a stick

range.description: Indigenous folk tradition is concentrated in northern Kyushu, especially Fukuoka Prefecture (former Chikuzen Province) and Ōita Prefecture. The figure is now nationally and internationally recognised through Mizuki Shigeru's manga.

hotspots.name: Onga County, Fukuoka Prefecture

location.description: Coastal northern Kyushu, in the former Chikuzen Province

hotspots.peak_period: Pre-modern folk tradition through 1930s ethnographic collection
hotspots.notes: Principal source area for Yanagita Kunio's documentation of the nurikabe legend

first_recorded.source: Yōkai picture scroll (Bakemono no e) held by Brigham Young University; first modern textual collection by Yanagita Kunio (1938)

peak_activity_periods.description: Iconographic depiction in yōkai scrolls (BYU c. 1660)
Ethnographic collection of regional folktales by Yanagita Kunio
Mass-cultural revival via Mizuki Shigeru's GeGeGe no Kitarō

origins.cultural_roots: Folk traditions of nighttime travelers in northern Kyushu, where invisible obstructions on country roads were attributed to a distinct yōkai.
origins.earliest_accounts: A c. 1660 Edo-period yōkai handscroll held by Brigham Young University depicts a creature explicitly labelled nurikabe; identified by Yumoto Kōichi and announced in 2007.
origins.folklore_connections: Member of the broader category of Japanese 'road yōkai' (michi no yōkai) that bedevil lone travelers, alongside nobiagari and betobeto-san.

timeline.event: Earliest known illustrated record: a yōkai handscroll labelled with the name 'nurikabe', later acquired by the L. Tom Perry Special Collections at Brigham Young University
timeline.significance: Pushes documented existence of the figure to the mid-Edo period

timeline.event: Folklorist Kunio Yanagita publishes accounts of nurikabe in folk-tale collections, locating it in Onga County, Fukuoka
Mizuki Shigeru's GeGeGe no Kitarō introduces the iconic anthropomorphic wall design
timeline.significance: Modern visual identity of nurikabe; the character becomes a member of Kitarō's troupe

timeline.event: Yumoto Kōichi identifies the c. 1660 BYU scroll's creature as a labelled nurikabe
timeline.significance: First confirmed pre-modern image of the yōkai

history.modern_era: Through GeGeGe no Kitarō, related anime, and Mizuki Shigeru's yōkai dictionaries, nurikabe has become one of Japan's most recognisable yōkai. The 2007 BYU rediscovery led to a small wave of academic and popular interest in pre-modern depictions and the history of the figure beyond Mizuki's design.

documentary.name: Bakemono no e (c. 1660), L. Tom Perry Special Collections
documentary.description: Edo-period yōkai handscroll containing an illustration explicitly labelled 'nurikabe', depicting a three-eyed dog-elephant-like creature.
documentary.location: Brigham Young University, Provo, Utah, USA
documentary.analysis: Identified as the earliest known visual record of the nurikabe by Yumoto Kōichi (announced 2007).

documentary.name: Yanagita Kunio's nurikabe accounts
documentary.description: Field-collected folk narratives placing nurikabe in Onga County, Fukuoka Prefecture, with the canonical 'tap the base with a stick' resolution.
documentary.analysis: Foundation for the 20th-century literary career of the yōkai.

paranormal.name: Genuine yōkai obstruction
paranormal.description: Traditional view that nurikabe is a discrete supernatural entity that impedes travelers as a manifestation of the night road's spiritual hazards.
evidence_cited: Multi-generational folk testimony recorded by Yanagita Kunio

scientific.name: Sensory disorientation in fatigued travelers
scientific.description: Reports correspond to nighttime disorientation, fatigue, low-visibility fog and ground mist on rural Kyushu roads, in which lone walkers lose their bearing and feel unable to proceed.
evidence_cited: Climatic conditions of coastal northern Kyushu
Comparable disorientation phenomena in other folk traditions

skeptical.name: Cultural construction by modern media
skeptical.description: While the folkloric kernel is genuine, the dominant mental image of nurikabe is a 20th-century creation by Mizuki Shigeru rather than an inherited visual tradition.
evidence_cited: Absence (until 2007) of any known pre-modern image
Direct testimony of Mizuki Shigeru on his New Guinea inspiration

traditions: Yōkai picture-scroll tradition of the Edo period
stories: Travelers in Onga County stopped on the road by an invisible wall, freed by sweeping a stick at its base
Mizuki Shigeru's wartime experience in New Guinea of an invisible obstruction
folklore.beliefs: Tradition interprets nighttime obstruction on lonely roads as a yōkai attack rather than mere disorientation; the stick-sweeping remedy is canonical.

literature: Mizuki Shigeru's Yōkai Daizukan and related compendia
film_tv: GeGeGe no Kitarō (multiple anime series, 1968 onward)
games: Nioh series — appearance as a yokai enemy
other: GeGeGe no Kitarō museum exhibits in Sakaiminato (Mizuki Shigeru Road)

researchers.name: Kunio Yanagita
researchers.contribution: First systematic publication of nurikabe folklore

researchers.name: Mizuki Shigeru
researchers.contribution: Created the dominant modern visual depiction of nurikabe

researchers.name: Yumoto Kōichi
researchers.affiliation: Yumoto Kōichi Memorial Japan Yokai Museum and yōkai scholar
researchers.contribution: Identification of the BYU c. 1660 nurikabe scroll

organizations.focus: Custodian of the c. 1660 nurikabe scroll

research.ongoing_studies: Continued cataloguing of Edo-period yōkai emaki and reassessment of pre-modern nurikabe iconography in the wake of the 2007 BYU rediscovery.
